query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-coating tungsten particles with a thin nickel layer will improve interfacial bonding with copper, which in turn reduces void formation and phase separation in the composite, leading to superior thermal transport and mechanical durability under fusion-reactor thermal flux and irradiation conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: W particles (or connected W regions) embedded in a Cu matrix made by conventional powder metallurgy or sintering techniques that typically suffer from residual voids and phase mismatch.
generation.intervention: Apply an electrolessly deposited, ultrathin nickel coating on the tungsten particles prior to incorporating them into a copper matrix.
generation.conditions: During sintering and subsequent service under fusion-relevant conditions (elevated temperatures up to ~1100 °C and exposure to irradiation similar to the doses examined in reported electron and ion tests).
generation.structural_mediator: An interfacial nickel layer that bridges between tungsten and copper.
generation.mechanism: Nickel acts as a wetting promoter and diffusion barrier, reducing surface energy differences between W and Cu. This enhanced wetting minimizes void formation and phase separation during sintering while preserving the mechanical continuity at the interface, which is vital under cyclic high-heat and irradiation loading.
generation.predicted_outcome: W–Cu composites fabricated with Ni-coated tungsten particles will display improved thermal conductivity and reduced interfacial defects, as well as maintained or improved mechanical durability compared to composites produced without the nickel coating.
generation.baseline: Conventional fabrication methods (e.g., spark-plasma sintering or vapor-coated W powders without interfacial modification) that typically result in microstructural defects and imperfect W–Cu contact.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective at processing temperatures up to those relevant for reactor component annealing (<1100 °C) and under irradiation conditions analogous to those tested in existing electron and ion irradiation experiments.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal thickness of the nickel layer and its long-term stability under high irradiation have yet to be determined; furthermore, scale-up effects or interactions with other inevitable processing impurities could influence performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composites: one set using tungsten particles pre-coated with a controlled, ultrathin nickel layer via electroless deposition and a control set using uncoated tungsten. Process both sets by identical sintering conditions representative of existing fabrication baselines. Subject the samples to a standardized irradiation protocol (e.g., electron or ion irradiation with fluences comparable to prior tests) and thermal cycling representative of reactor service.
measurements: High-resolution electron microscopy to quantify void formation and interfacial bonding quality
Thermal conductivity measurements before and after irradiation and thermal cycling
Mechanical testing (e.g., fracture toughness, cyclic loading) to evaluate durability
Phase analysis (XRD/EDS) to assess any irradiation-induced interfacial phase changes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-coated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in thermal conductivity, interfacial integrity (i.e., fewer voids or defects), and mechanical performance compared to the uncoated controls under identical irradiation and thermal conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractIn fusion reactors, such as ITER or DEMO, the plasma used to generate nuclear reactions will reach temperatures that are an order of magnitude higher than in the Sun’s core. Although the plasma is not supposed to be in contact with the reactor walls, a large amount of heat generated by electromagnetic radiation, electrons and ions being expelled from the plasma will reach the plasma-facing surface of the reactor. Especially for the divertor part, high heat fluxes of up to 20 MW/m2 are expected even in normal operating conditions. An improvement in the plasma-facing material (which is, in the case of ITER, pure Tungsten, W) is desired at least in terms of both a higher recrystallization temperature and a lower brittle-to-ductile transition temperature. In the present work, we discuss three microengineering routes based on inclusions of nanometric dispersions, which are proposed to improve the W properties, and present the microstructural and thermophysical properties of the resulting W-based composites with such dispersions. The materials’ behavior after 6 MeV electron irradiation tests is also presented, and their further development is discussed.Keywords: mater

## Abstract
AbstractNuclear fusion is a promising energy source. The International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor aims to study the feasibility of tokamak-type reactors and test technologies and materials for commercial use. One major challenge is developing materials for the reactor’s divertor, which supports high thermal flux. Tungsten was chosen as the plasma-facing material, while a CuCrZr alloy will be used in the cooling pipes. However, the gradient between the working temperatures of these materials requires the use of a thermal barrier interlayer between them. To this end, refractory high-entropy (CrFeTiTa)70W30 and VFeTiTaW alloys were prepared by mechanical alloying and sintering, and their thermal and irradiation resistance was evaluated. Both alloys showed phase growth after annealing at 1100 °C for 8 days, being more pronounced for higher temperatures (1300 °C and 1500 °C). The VFeTiTaW alloy presented greater phase growth, suggesting lower microstructural stability, however, no new phases were formed.
